title: What We Talk About When We Talk About the Love of Reading
author: Shanahan, Timothy
summary: Timothy Shanahan reviews alarming data on declining reading pleasure—35% of K-12 students dislike reading, only 14% of 8th graders read for enjoyment daily—and asks what schools can actually do about it. His core argument is that reading decline has structural causes that began in the 1940s, not with smartphones, and that teaching 'love of reading' directly is not a well-defined or evidence-supported instructional goal. What matters is ensuring all children achieve real reading proficiency, because proficiency is the prerequisite for pleasure.
points: Reading for pleasure has been in structural decline since the 1940s—not since smartphones—revealing that the causes are deeper than any single technology.

35% of K-12 students dislike reading, 43% never read for fun, and only 14% of 8th graders read for enjoyment daily; college graduates—traditionally the highest reading group—have declined sharply since 2003.
Teaching students to love reading is not a well-defined instructional objective; the honest goal is teaching them to read with genuine proficiency, since proficiency is what makes pleasure possible.
Reading decline correlates with increased leisure time among groups that were not historically socialised into books—demographic shifts in who attends college, not just screen competition.
Schools cannot compensate for the full range of social and structural forces driving reading decline, but ensuring all children achieve genuine reading proficiency is within their reach.
The most rigorous analysis of reading decline (Bone et al., 2025) confirms the 1940s starting point, revealing that framing this as a recent crisis misrepresents a long-running structural trend.
quotes: That’s provocative, but it neglects that such teaching was universal in the 1940s and 1950s when people read more ((e.g., Dick & Jane, Alice & Jerry), and that a steady decline in pleasure reading accompanied the massive increase book-based reading instruction that took place in the 1990s-2010s (e.g., whole language, Guided Reading, Accelerated Reader, Units of Study).

Adults (25-54) have experienced no improvements in time availability since the 1940s, but young adults and senior citizens both have more leisure time (14-25-year-olds gained 5 hours per week, and the seniors have 14 hours more weekly (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024; Krantz-Kent & Stewart, 2007).

Perhaps this shift in reading habits by college graduates is a mirror of what has been documented in our universities, that students are not even doing the reading required in their coursework (Baier, 2011) – though this group’s interest in pleasure reading has long been dubious (Jersild, 1931).

That’s why – if we want to have a society with lots of readers and reading – it matters that we ensure that our schools teach all children to read with great proficiency, that our communities have libraries, and that our tax and mailing policies keep texts of all kinds affordable and accessible.

In the most rigorous and inciteful analysis of all this, it’s noted that our reading decline started in 1940s – not the 2000s (Bone, Bu, Sonke, & Francourt, 2025; Canoy, van Ours, & van der Ploeg, 2006; James & Moore, 1940; National Endowment for the Arts, 2007; Robinson, 1980).

The American Academy of the Arts and Sciences (2023) reports that 84% of adults read for 5 minutes or less on a typical day – only 19% devote such a small amount of time to watching television, playing games, and using computers for personal purposes.
